KEY MESSAGE 1... 
The remnant low of Isaias is centered over West 
Virginia this afternoon, while a weak mid/upper trough axis that has 
been helping to steer the remnants is centered over the southern 
Great Lakes and Ohio Valley. As the trough axis progresses east 
tonight, the remnant low will be transported east into the Mid 
Atlantic region before exiting offshore Monday morning. 

The bulk of the rain has shifted into central PA, but abundant low-
level moisture and some PVA from the mid/upper trough overhead is 
keeping bands of light showers and drizzle from north central Ohio 
through NE Ohio and NW PA. This light shower activity and drizzle 
will gradually pivot east this evening and tonight, but given the 
amount of low-level moisture lingering beneath the trough axis, feel 
that drizzle will be stubborn to end even after the actual rain 
showers end. Trended the forecast toward longer periods of drizzle 
and mist gradually ending from west to east through 06Z tonight, but 
low clouds and patchy fog are likely all night. Drying of the 
boundary layer in the wake of the trough should gradually break up 
the low clouds Monday morning, and expect increasing sunshine by 
afternoon as mid/upper ridging expands over the central and eastern 
CONUS and surface high pressure strengthens across the Appalachians 
and SE CONUS in response to deep mid/upper troughing progressing 
further into the western CONUS. This will set up increasing warm air 
advection to boost highs well above normal Monday afternoon, with 
upper 70s/low 80s in NW Ohio and low/mid 70s in NE Ohio and NW PA.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
The warmth that starts Monday afternoon will really 
peak Tuesday as the mid/upper ridge further amplifies over the 
eastern CONUS ahead of the western trough evolving into a closed low 
near the Four Corners region. Strengthening warm/moist advection and 
isentropic ascent combined with a mid/upper shortwave and surface 
low crossing the central Great Lakes could drive a few showers north 
of a retreating warm front Monday night into early Tuesday morning. 
These could brush the lakeshore counties of northern Ohio and NW PA, 
but the bulk of any rain should be over Lake Erie and southern 
Ontario. Impressive warmth is likely in the warm sector Tuesday 
afternoon, with probabilities increasing for record highs in parts 
of the region as temperatures reach the mid 80s in NW and north 
central Ohio and upper 70s/low 80s in NE Ohio and NW PA. The best 
chance to exceed the records will be at KTOL and KCLE. See climate 
section for details. 

The ridge will start to flatten Tuesday evening and night as a 
northern stream mid/upper trough drops across the central and 
eastern Great Lakes. This will push a cold front slowly south into 
the area Tuesday night, but the front will become quasi-stationary 
late Tuesday night into Wednesday morning as the combination of 
strong ridging to the south and energy emanating out of the 
Four Corners closed low riding the boundary holds it up. A few 
showers and thunderstorms could occur late Tuesday afternoon and
evening in NE Ohio and NW PA as forcing increases ahead of the 
approaching shortwave and 110+ knot jet, but the bulk of the 
rain will occur late Tuesday night into Wednesday as the 
boundary gradually sags south and the energy from the west rides
along it. The sagging front and precip will keep temperatures 
cooler Wednesday, with highs in the upper 60s/low 70s north and 
low/mid 70s south.

KEY MESSAGE 3...
The front will briefly push into the Ohio Valley 
Wednesday night and early Thursday as Canadian high pressure ridges 
down from the Upper Great Lakes leading to seasonably cool and drier 
conditions. However, the front will quickly lift back north as a 
warm front late Thursday and Thursday night ahead of a potentially 
significant storm system. The old Four Corners cut off low will 
attempt to phase with a strong northern stream mid/upper trough 
diving into the northern Plains and Upper Midwest Thursday night and 
Friday, resulting in a rapidly deepening surface low crossing the 
Lower Great Lakes Friday and strong cold frontal passage. There 
remains uncertainty on the strength of this system and resultant 
push of cold air in its wake due to differences in how much the 
northern stream trough can phase with the old cut off low, but 
ensemble guidance and general pattern recognition suggests at least 
a seasonably strong Fall storm system and the coldest air of the 
season so far. Widespread rain is likely Friday followed by falling 
temperatures late Friday into Saturday and lingering lake effect 
showers. Depending on the strength of this system, wind headlines 
are certainly possible. Slow moderation by Sunday.
